RagShortTexts: The economic sustenance of Armenia in 374 AD relied upon extensive agrarian estates, pastoral herds, and strategic mineral extraction.
Anchored around commercial hubs near Vagharshapat & Artashat, merchant caravans traded valuable bullion, grain, wine, and exotic raw goods.
Advanced weapon smithies and metallurgical workshops provided the industrial backbone necessary to equip large armies in the field.

Variants.Content: Underpinning the immense martial demands of Armenia was an agrarian and mercantile economic system rooted in rural estates and municipal workshops. Across fertile valleys and pastures, countless tenant farmers and laborers produced wheat harvests, vintage wines, cured pelts, and high-grade iron ingots destined for storehouses. Within thriving market plazas around Vagharshapat & Artashat, cosmopolitan merchants converged to barter gold coinage, imported silks, fine armaments, and livestock. Imperial or royal customs officials maintained toll gates, extracting heavy excise duties from freight wagons. Yet the system faced constant vulnerability from harvest failures and trade route disruptions, compelling rulers to enforce grain requisitions to sustain armies in the field.

Muleteers in the highland valleys lead laden donkeys up slick trails, and the watch officer's lantern shows that the grain reserve is only half of what the tally promised. Legionaries in iron scale coats trade spare arrows for leather straps, while the paymaster haggles over whether silver or wine will clear the arrears.

The house estate near the capital counts its sheep and wine casks, and the report from the toll gate reads poorly. Write to the Iberian merchants in private, offering reduced tithes on their caravans in return for loans against the spring harvest. Send the letter by your own courier and keep it sealed, because the king's fiscal agents read every ledger they can reach.
